name: Brute force response
description:
A first-responder checklist for a credential-guessing incident: establish whether anything succeeded before deciding how urgent this is, then contain and follow up.
Note the two steps carrying `intended_*` fields. Those name an action rather than binding to a catalog entry, and they will import as ordinary manual tasks on your deployment — wire them to your own automation deliberately, which is also the moment to think about whether that response should be allowed to run unattended.

name: Authentik authentication object deletion burst
description:
Five or more authentik objects deleted inside thirty minutes. Legitimate administration removes flows, policies, providers and stages one at a time; a burst is either a blueprint rollback or someone dismantling the authentication path ahead of an intrusion.

Ungrouped by design - `correlation_key: none`. The actor is in `data.dstuser`, but the detection is about the estate, not the operator, and a burst split across two admin accounts is more alarming rather than less.

Volume: 35 deletions in 30 days on the reference deployment, never more than two in any half hour.

Requires a decoder named `authentik` emitting the `policy_changed` rule group.

name: Authentik brute force from a single source
description:
Repeated failed sign-ins to an authentik identity provider from one address inside a short window. Covers both halves of credential guessing: `login_failed` (known user, wrong secret) and `invalid_identifier` (username does not resolve at all), which authentik reports as distinct actions.

The `data.event: "Created Event"` condition is load-bearing, not decoration. authentik emits three separate records for one failed sign-in - the audit event, a policy-stage `Invalid credentials` line, and a reputation `Updated score` line - and all three carry the `authentication_failed` group. Counting the group alone therefore triples every threshold, and two of the three carry no client address at all. `Created Event` selects only the audit record: one per attempt, always addressed.

Volume: the reference deployment saw 6 failed sign-ins in 30 days across ~40 accounts, so 10 in 15 minutes is roughly two orders of magnitude above baseline and has never fired unprompted. An internet-facing IdP will need a higher count.

Requires a decoder named `authentik` emitting the `authentication_failed` rule group, and the client address in `data.srcip`. authentik logs the address as `client_ip`, which is a dynamic field, so it must be mapped into the `srcip` static field at the shipping layer for this to match. See Portability in the pull request.

name: Authentik impersonation followed by secret access
description:
An administrator starting an impersonation session and then reading a token or certificate secret within the hour. Impersonation is a legitimate support tool, and reading a secret is a legitimate administrative act; the sequence is what is worth seeing, because impersonation moves the operator into someone else's authorisation context before the secret is read.

Volume: 3 impersonations and 8 secret reads in 30 days on the reference deployment; the sequence never observed.

Requires a decoder named `authentik` emitting the `impersonation_started` and `secret_view` audit actions.

name: Authentik MFA device removed then password set by the same operator
description:
An authenticator device deleted and a password set by the same operator inside an hour - the account-takeover sequence, whether run by a compromised admin session or by an attacker who already holds a session and is removing the second factor before persisting.

Correlates on the operator (`data.dstuser`), not the victim: authentik records the acting user on the audit event and the affected object under `data.context.model`, which is not a correlation key. A helpdesk agent legitimately resetting an account will match this, so treat it as an event worth a question rather than an incident.

Volume: 1 password_set in 30 days on the reference deployment; the pair never observed.

Requires a decoder named `authentik` emitting audit actions and `data.context.model.app`.

name: Authentik password spraying from a single source
description:
One address attempting sign-in against many different accounts - the low-and-slow inverse of brute force, where each account sees too few failures to trip a per-account threshold.

The `data.event: "Created Event"` condition is load-bearing, not decoration. authentik emits three separate records for one failed sign-in - the audit event, a policy-stage `Invalid credentials` line, and a reputation `Updated score` line - and all three carry the `authentication_failed` group. Counting the group alone therefore triples every threshold, and two of the three carry no client address at all. `Created Event` selects only the audit record: one per attempt, always addressed.

The diversity constraint is what separates this from rule-1 brute force: ten failures against one account is guessing, ten against five accounts is enumeration.

Volume: never observed on the reference deployment in 30 days.

Requires a decoder named `authentik` emitting the `authentication_failed` rule group, and the client address in `data.srcip`. authentik logs the address as `client_ip`, which is a dynamic field, so it must be mapped into the `srcip` static field at the shipping layer for this to match. See Portability in the pull request.

name: Authentik secret enumeration by a single operator
description:
Five or more token or certificate secrets read by one operator inside fifteen minutes. Reading one secret is administration; sweeping the store is collection, and is what an attacker does with a stolen admin session before moving laterally to whatever those tokens authenticate.

Volume: 8 secret reads in 30 days on the reference deployment, never more than two together.

Requires a decoder named `authentik` emitting the `secret_view` audit action.

name: Authentik successful sign-in after repeated failures from one source
description:
A run of failed sign-ins from one address followed by a success from that same address - the shape of credential guessing that worked, and the highest-value single detection an identity provider can offer.

The `data.event: "Created Event"` condition is load-bearing, not decoration. authentik emits three separate records for one failed sign-in - the audit event, a policy-stage `Invalid credentials` line, and a reputation `Updated score` line - and all three carry the `authentication_failed` group. Counting the group alone therefore triples every threshold, and two of the three carry no client address at all. `Created Event` selects only the audit record: one per attempt, always addressed.

Correlates on address rather than username deliberately. authentik records the *submitted* identifier on a failure (often an email) and the *canonical* username on success, so the two legs frequently disagree about who the user is; keying on `user.name` would silently never join. Verified on live data 2026-08-19.

Volume: never observed on the reference deployment. Expect occasional benign hits from a user who mistypes a password several times and then succeeds - tune leg 0 upward if that is common in your estate.

Requires a decoder named `authentik` emitting the `authentication_failed` rule group, and the client address in `data.srcip`. authentik logs the address as `client_ip`, which is a dynamic field, so it must be mapped into the `srcip` static field at the shipping layer for this to match. See Portability in the pull request.

name: Failed mail logins followed by a successful login from the same source
description:
A source address that fails mailbox authentication several times and then succeeds inside the same window. This is the moment a credential-guessing run stops being an attempt and becomes an intrusion, and it is the single highest-value correlation on a mail server: a mailbox is enough to read everything the account has ever received and to send as that person.
The two legs are deliberately allowed to come from different decoders. On a typical Mailu deployment the failures surface on the edge proxy while the success is logged by the mailbox server behind it, so pinning both legs to one decoder name would make the rule unfirable. Both legs are scoped by `decoder.name contains mailu` and share the `source.ip` correlation key.
Requires decoders whose names contain `mailu` emitting the stock `authentication_failed` and `authentication_success` rule groups with `data.srcip` populated on both — see Portability in the pull request. Without them this artifact imports cleanly and never fires.
Volume: zero findings over six days on the reference deployment. Every one of 6,577 successful mailbox logins in that period came from an internal address, while every failure came from the internet, so the two legs never shared a source. That is the expected steady state — this rule is meant to be silent, and a single finding is worth waking someone for.

name: FortiGate Firewall Login Outside Office Hours
description: This rule detects logins to a fortigate firewall outside normal office hours.

name: Incoming Port Scan from Internet (Fortigate Outside Interface)
description: Rule detects a incomming port scan from the internet, triggers when more than 300 distinct ports have been scanned.

name: Low-and-slow password spraying against a mail service
description:
One source address failing authentication against many different mailboxes over hours rather than seconds. This is spraying (T1110.003) rather than brute force: the attacker walks a dictionary of likely local parts — info@, support@, admin@, test@, webmaster@ — trying one or two passwords each, and never generates the burst that a rate-based rule looks for.
The window is deliberately six hours. On the reference deployment the actor that motivated this rule averaged well under one attempt per fifteen minutes and never touched more than three distinct mailboxes in any single hour. A conventional "N failures in 15 minutes" rule — including the SSH brute-force artifact in this same repo — is completely silent against it. What separates the attacker from ordinary users is not rate, it is the number of *distinct* accounts, which is why the leg keys on min_distinct rather than on count alone.
Requires a decoder whose name contains `mailu` emitting the stock `authentication_failed` rule group with `data.srcip` and `data.dstuser` populated — see Portability in the pull request. Any mail decoder that does the same satisfies it; without one this artifact imports cleanly and never fires.
Volume: over a six-day window on a single-domain mail server, one source produced 282 failed authentications across 54 distinct mailboxes, reaching 14 distinct mailboxes inside a single six-hour window. Every other source in the same period reached at most 3, and all but one reached exactly 1. A threshold of 8 separates them with room on both sides. Expect one finding per spraying source, not per attempt.

name: Mailbox authenticating from a previously unseen source address
description:
A mailbox logging in successfully from an address it has never used before, judged against a thirty-day per-account baseline. This is the detection that survives a stolen password: the credential is valid, the login succeeds, nothing fails, and the only thing that is unusual is where it came from.
It is deliberately a novelty rule and not a counting rule. Counting distinct source addresses per account does not work on real mail users — on the reference deployment one ordinary account legitimately authenticated from eleven different addresses in six days through roaming between mobile and fixed networks, while two other accounts used exactly one each. Any count threshold high enough to clear the roaming user is far above anything an attacker needs. Novelty against that account's own history is the discriminator, and `baseline_lookback_days` is what makes it one.
Expect noise proportional to how much your users travel, and treat the severity as a triage hint rather than a verdict. Pair it with the geolocation your platform already has if you have it; a new address in the same city is not the same finding as a new address on another continent.
Requires a decoder whose name contains `mailu` emitting the stock `authentication_success` rule group with `data.dstuser` and `data.srcip` populated — see Portability in the pull request. Without it this artifact imports cleanly and never fires.
Volume: on the reference deployment 6,577 successful logins over six days resolved to 13 distinct source addresses across 3 accounts. After the thirty-day baseline is warm this should produce a finding only when someone genuinely appears from somewhere new, which for a stable estate is a handful per month.

name: Multiple failed logins followed by a succes full login on vaultwarden.
description:
Alerts triggers when multiple failed logins are followed by a successfull login to vaultwarden from the same source ip address.
Requires vaultwarden logging, successfull 100201 and failed 100202.

name: One source refused by several independent reverse-proxy controls
description:
A single source address refused by three or more DIFFERENT access-control plugins inside the same window - for example a DNS blocklist hit, then a user-agent blacklist, then a behavioural ban. Each control answers a different question about the caller: where it has been, what it claims to be, and what it has just been doing. One of them refusing a request is routine and enormously common. Three independent ones refusing the same address inside a few minutes means the caller is failing every test the proxy has, which no ordinary client does.
The diversity constraint is the whole rule. `min_distinct` is applied to the field naming which control fired, so a thousand refusals from one blocklist never satisfy it - only breadth across controls does. That makes this rule insensitive to the volume of whichever blocklist happens to be loudest on a given estate, which is what makes a fixed threshold portable at all.
Requires a decoder whose name contains `bunkerweb` emitting an `invalid_access` rule group with `data.srcip` and `data.bw_deny_source` populated, where `bw_deny_source` names the plugin that refused the request - see Portability in the pull request. `data.bw_deny_source` is specific to a BunkerWeb decoder; on any other reverse proxy the equivalent field will be named differently and this artifact will import cleanly and never fire.
Scoping note (revision 2): the legs scope to the application with `rule.groups contains bunkerweb`, NOT `decoder.name contains bunkerweb`. On a Wazuh alerts index `decoder.name` is a **keyword** field, so a `contains` condition compiles to a `match` query that requires the WHOLE term - it matches a decoder named exactly `bunkerweb` and never `bunkerweb-accesslog`, `bunkerweb-modsec` or `bunkerweb-plugin`, which is where every event this rule wants actually lives. Revision 1 had that bug and could not fire at all; measured against a live index, the two conditions it required intersected on zero documents. The application name is carried as a rule GROUP on every rule of the family, and matches correctly as an exact term inside that array.
Volume: zero on the reference deployment. Every one of 321 refusals in the sample window came from the DNS blocklist alone, so no address ever tripped a second control. This rule is meant to be silent, and that silence is itself informative - it says the first control is catching things before the others get a chance to.

name: Repeated sign-in attempts against the BunkerWeb admin console
description:
Several sign-in attempts against the BunkerWeb web UI from one source address inside a short window. That console configures every access-control policy the reverse proxy enforces - blacklists, rate limits, WAF settings, TLS - so an account on it is worth more than an account on anything sitting behind it. It should see a handful of sign-ins a week from a small set of known addresses, and nothing else.
The leg counts ATTEMPTS, not failures, and that is deliberate. BunkerWeb logs the attempt before the outcome is known - `Login attempt from <ip> with username "<user>"` - and what it prints on a failed sign-in is not documented. A leg written against a guessed failure string is a rule that passes review, imports cleanly and never fires; counting attempts needs no such guess and cannot silently rot if the failure wording changes. The cost is that five legitimate sign-ins in ten minutes would also fire, which on an admin console is itself worth a look.
Requires a decoder whose name contains `bunkerweb` emitting an `authentication_attempt` rule group with `data.srcip` populated - see Portability in the pull request. Without it this artifact imports cleanly and never fires.
Scoping note (revision 2): the legs scope to the application with `rule.groups contains bunkerweb`, NOT `decoder.name contains bunkerweb`. On a Wazuh alerts index `decoder.name` is a **keyword** field, so a `contains` condition compiles to a `match` query that requires the WHOLE term - it matches a decoder named exactly `bunkerweb` and never `bunkerweb-accesslog`, `bunkerweb-modsec` or `bunkerweb-plugin`, which is where every event this rule wants actually lives. Revision 1 had that bug and could not fire at all; measured against a live index, the two conditions it required intersected on zero documents. The application name is carried as a rule GROUP on every rule of the family, and matches correctly as an exact term inside that array.
Volume: one attempt in fourteen days on the reference deployment, from an internal address. This rule is meant to be silent, and a single finding is worth acting on.

name: SSH brute force from a single source
description:
Repeated failed SSH authentication from one source address within a short window — the classic credential-guessing shape. Built entirely on stock Wazuh sshd rule ids (5710 "attempt to login using a non-existent user" and 5716 "authentication failed"), so it is portable to any deployment running the default ruleset with no local rules required.
Tune `count` to your estate before enabling: 20 in 15 minutes is deliberately conservative and will stay quiet on most networks. A perimeter host exposed to the internet will see this constantly from background noise, which is why the Backtest number matters more than the default.

name: Web enumeration followed by exploitation from the same source
description:
A source address that first enumerates paths on a site and then sends a request the WAF recognises as an actual attack payload - SQL injection, cross-site scripting, command execution, remote or local file inclusion. Enumeration on its own is the background noise of the public internet. Enumeration that turns into exploitation is somebody acting on what they found, and that is a different event.
The two legs are deliberately keyed on different rule groups rather than different severities. `web_scan` is set by the rules that answer "is this file here?" and "who is asking?"; `exploit_attempt` is set by the rules that answer "do this to the target". Both would otherwise carry only a generic `attack` group, and a leg condition has no negation - so a source that merely probed for `/.env` would satisfy both legs and the rule would fire on plain scanning, which is precisely what it exists to filter out.
Requires a decoder whose name contains `bunkerweb` emitting BOTH the `web_scan` and `exploit_attempt` rule groups with `data.srcip` populated, and keeping those two groups disjoint - see Portability in the pull request. Without that separation this artifact degrades into the enumeration rule, and without the groups it imports cleanly and never fires.
Scoping note (revision 2): the legs scope to the application with `rule.groups contains bunkerweb`, NOT `decoder.name contains bunkerweb`. On a Wazuh alerts index `decoder.name` is a **keyword** field, so a `contains` condition compiles to a `match` query that requires the WHOLE term - it matches a decoder named exactly `bunkerweb` and never `bunkerweb-accesslog`, `bunkerweb-modsec` or `bunkerweb-plugin`, which is where every event this rule wants actually lives. Revision 1 had that bug and could not fire at all; measured against a live index, the two conditions it required intersected on zero documents. The application name is carried as a rule GROUP on every rule of the family, and matches correctly as an exact term inside that array.
Volume: on the reference deployment - one internet-facing reverse proxy in front of roughly forty sites - three of eight enumerating sources also tripped a WAF attack rule inside a forty-five minute sample. Expect this to be materially rarer than enumeration alone, and to be worth looking at when it fires.

name: Web path enumeration from a single source
description:
One source address requesting many distinct paths that have no legitimate caller - dotfiles and source control (`/.env`, `/.git/config`), credential files, CMS and admin panels, PHP entry points. Individually each request is a shrug: it was refused, or it 404ed, and one of them means nothing. The pattern is the finding, which is why this belongs in a scheduled search rather than in a per-event rule.
The leg selects the `web_scan` group rather than a status code, so it fires whether the reverse proxy blocked the request, the application 404ed it, or - worst case - it was served. What separates a sweep from a person mistyping a URL is the diversity constraint: at least ten DISTINCT paths inside the window, not just ten requests. A retry loop against one path never satisfies it.
Requires a decoder whose name contains `bunkerweb` emitting the `web_scan` rule group with `data.srcip` and `data.url` populated - see Portability in the pull request. Without it this artifact imports cleanly and never fires.
Scoping note (revision 2): the legs scope to the application with `rule.groups contains bunkerweb`, NOT `decoder.name contains bunkerweb`. On a Wazuh alerts index `decoder.name` is a **keyword** field, so a `contains` condition compiles to a `match` query that requires the WHOLE term - it matches a decoder named exactly `bunkerweb` and never `bunkerweb-accesslog`, `bunkerweb-modsec` or `bunkerweb-plugin`, which is where every event this rule wants actually lives. Revision 1 had that bug and could not fire at all; measured against a live index, the two conditions it required intersected on zero documents. The application name is carried as a rule GROUP on every rule of the family, and matches correctly as an exact term inside that array.
Volume: on the reference deployment - one internet-facing reverse proxy in front of roughly forty sites - nine distinct source addresses satisfied this in a forty-five minute sample, sweeping between 18 and 283 distinct paths each. Expect findings continuously on any estate exposed to the internet; that is the steady state of the public web, and the value here is one finding per sweep instead of several hundred individual alerts. Tighten `min_distinct` if your estate is noisier.
